content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a retention rate of over 85% at 12 months as a target for good performance, while rates between 75% and 85% are considered fair, and rates below 75% are deemed poor. Retention monitoring is particularly important for pregnant and breastfeeding women due to the increased risk of HIV transmission to their infants. These women require more frequent and earlier retention assessments compared to the general population. Early retention indicators can help identify women who are lost to follow-up (LTF), which is most common by the second antenatal care (ANC) visit. Retention data for these women is typically collected at one and six months after initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART). To monitor retention effectively, ART registers should be maintained in all settings where ART is provided. In maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) settings, specific ART registers may simplify data collection. Otherwise, the pregnancy or breastfeeding status of women is recorded in the ART follow-up columns. The numerator for retention calculations includes the number of pregnant or breastfeeding women alive and on ART at one and six months after starting treatment, while the denominator includes all such women who initiated ART during the same period. Retention monitoring is essential for all pregnant women on ART, regardless of when they started treatment. Some women may already be on ART when they become pregnant, while others may start treatment during pregnancy. Countries are encouraged to monitor retention for all pregnant women on ART, treating ANC enrollment as the starting point for care. Lost-to-follow-up (LTF) patients are those who miss clinic appointments by more than 90 days. However, being classified as LTF does not necessarily mean the patient is no longer in care or on ART. LTF patients may include those who have died, transferred to another facility, or are alive but not in care. It is recommended that HIV programs investigate the true outcomes of LTF patients and re-engage those who are alive but not in care. This process often involves community follow-up to reclassify outcomes and improve retention rates. Retention rates can vary significantly within the first 12 months of ART initiation, often due to delayed treatment initiation and higher mortality among patients with advanced HIV infection. Strengthening early ART initiation is critical to improving survival during this period. Disaggregating retention data by population and location can help identify specific groups or regions with higher mortality rates. Viral load suppression is a key indicator of ART success. This indicator is critical for assessing the effectiveness of HIV treatment programs and achieving the third 90 goal of the UNAIDS 90-90-90 targets. Viral load monitoring should be routine, with a testing coverage of at least 75%. However, in settings with lower coverage, program-based denominators may be used, focusing on patients who have received viral load tests. Retention and viral load suppression data are essential for understanding the outcomes of HIV treatment programs. These indicators help identify gaps in care, improve patient outcomes, and reduce HIV transmission. Programs should prioritize efforts to retain patients in care, monitor viral load suppression, and address barriers to treatment adherence, such as transportation challenges, stigma, and lack of education about the importance of consistent care.
